name: Gemcitabine
route_note: IV infusion over 30 minutes, weekly or on days 1 and 8 of cycles

discovery.by: Larry Hertel and colleagues, Eli Lilly
discovery.note: Originally synthesised as a potential antiviral; antitumour activity was found during screening.

tagline: Difluorinated cytidine analogue used in pancreatic, lung, bladder and breast cancer
summary: Gemcitabine is a deoxycytidine analogue that, once phosphorylated, inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and is incorporated into DNA, terminating synthesis. It has broad solid-tumour activity and is a standard drug for pancreatic, lung, bladder, biliary, ovarian and breast cancer.
mechanism: Gemcitabine enters cells via nucleoside transporters and is phosphorylated by deoxycytidine kinase to its diphosphate and triphosphate.

The diphosphate inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, depleting deoxynucleotide pools; the triphosphate is incorporated into DNA, after which one more nucleotide is added before polymerisation stops ('masked chain termination'), shielding it from excision repair.
This self-potentiation and resistance to repair give it activity in solid tumours where cytarabine is inactive.
uses: Pancreatic cancer (alone, with nab-paclitaxel or capecitabine)

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Hertel's group at Lilly synthesises gemcitabine.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Approved as Gemzar for advanced pancreatic cancer.

history.title: Pancreatic trial
history.detail: Burris et al. publish that gemcitabine improves clinical benefit and survival over fluorouracil in pancreatic cancer.

history.title: Lung cancer
history.detail: FDA approves gemcitabine with cisplatin for NSCLC.

history.title: ABC-02
history.detail: Gemcitabine plus cisplatin becomes standard for advanced biliary tract cancer.

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Generic gemcitabine becomes available in the US after patent expiry.

history.title: MPACT
history.detail: Nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine extends survival in metastatic pancreatic cancer.

facts: Longer infusion times increase toxicity without clear benefit, so the 30-minute infusion is standard.
